content: The process of re-engaging individuals into HIV treatment programs is evaluated through key outcomes such as retention in care, viral suppression, treatment discontinuation, loss to follow-up, and mortality. A critical function of a national health information system (HIS) is to determine the number and percentage of people living with HIV (PLHIV) who are currently on antiretroviral therapy (ART) at any given time. This is based on the number of newly initiated ART patients and the attrition rates among those previously or newly reported to be on ART. These data must be analyzed at subnational levels and across relevant sociodemographic and priority populations. To accurately determine the number of PLHIV on ART, it is necessary to assess all programmatic outcome categories, including attrition categories such as death, treatment cessation, and loss to follow-up, at both the facility and individual patient levels. Official transfers-out are included in the count of PLHIV on ART who are considered alive and on treatment during the reporting period, as they are not classified under attrition categories. Unique identification of PLHIV within electronic HIS is the most effective way to identify unofficial or silent transfers between health facilities, which could impact overall retention figures. All countries should be able to report the number of PLHIV on ART within their national programs at a specific time point. To achieve this, it is essential to support HIS and the human resources required to manage these systems at all levels of the health sector. Routine monitoring of ART adherence and related data on the prevention of HIV drug resistance is described in WHO guidelines on person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance. Longitudinal patient outcome analyses, such as cohort studies examining short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes, are particularly useful at the facility level. Electronic data systems facilitate these analyses by enabling the tracking of patients across healthcare contacts through unique identifiers. Definitions for tracking ART care include: New ART patients: These include treatment-naïve individuals, non-naïve patients who previously received ART outside the formal healthcare system, and those who reinitiated ART after stopping treatment or being classified as lost to follow-up. PLHIV on ART: This includes patients who started ART at a facility, those transferred in, minus those transferred out, deceased, lost to follow-up, or who stopped ART. These numbers are aggregated across facilities for a national total. Total attrition from ART: This includes documented deaths, treatment cessation, and loss to follow-up. Deaths are defined as PLHIV previously on ART who have died from any cause. Treatment cessation refers to patients who stop their antiretroviral regimen, often in consultation with healthcare providers. Loss to follow-up is defined as 28 days or more since the last missed appointment or ARV refill. Toxicity monitoring has become a critical component of HIV treatment and prevention programs due to the prolonged exposure to antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) across all age groups, including pregnant and breastfeeding women. Although newer ARVs have more favorable toxicity profiles, ARV-associated toxicities remain a common reason for ART non-adherence, treatment discontinuation, or drug substitution. WHO recommends integrating toxicity monitoring into national monitoring and evaluation frameworks and including active ARV toxicity monitoring in routine HIV patient monitoring. This includes surveillance of ARV drug safety during pregnancy, monitoring congenital anomalies, and assessing the impact on growth and development in infants and young children exposed to ARVs via breast milk. Monitoring ART toxicity provides data on the incidence, clinical significance, and types of serious ARV toxicities, as well as their impact on patient outcomes and attrition. This information can guide strategies to prevent and mitigate drug toxicity, optimizing patient retention and viral load suppression (VLS) on treatment. Collecting data on programmatic reasons for ART switches or interruptions is also recommended, as this can inform strategies to improve adherence and retention. At the national level, ART coverage should be routinely reported at subnational levels and across sociodemographic groups. Disaggregating ART indicators by key populations and priority groups can uncover barriers to service access. Viral load suppression (VLS) is a critical measure of ART program success, reflecting the efficacy of drugs used and levels of retention and adherence among PLHIV. Routine viral load testing data provide vital information about program quality and effectiveness. Monitoring efforts to scale up viral load testing should be prioritized, as this data is essential for evaluating treatment success and transmission prevention. In the context of tuberculosis (TB) and HIV co-infection, TB remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality among PLHIV, even in the era of ART scale-up. Early ART initiation and retention are crucial for reducing mortality among TB patients. National TB and HIV programs must collaborate to ensure integrated, high-quality services. The cascade of care for HIV-associated TB depends on whether a person enters the health system for HIV or TB. Monitoring the implementation of newer WHO-approved diagnostic tools and ensuring routine cascade data reviews are essential for improving outcomes and impact.
